title: Control flow, switch expressions & patterns
summary: Arrow-form switch expressions with yield and no fall-through, the old colon switch, switch on strings and enums, pattern matching for instanceof, sealed hierarchies, and guard clauses.

quiz.prompt: What does `switch (404) { case 200, 201 -> "ok"; case 404 -> "missing"; default -> "other"; }` produce?
choices: `"missing"`
`"other"`
It does not compile
quiz.explanation: Arrow arms are checked against the selector and 404 matches its own constant arm, so the result is "missing". The "ok" arm lists only 200 and 201, default is used only when no arm matches, and comma-separated labels with arrows have been legal since Java 14, so the code compiles.

quiz.prompt: In the OLD colon-style switch, `case 1:` has no `break` and is followed by `case 2: ...; break;`. What runs for n == 1?
choices: Only case 1, which then exits the switch
Case 1 and then the default arm
Only case 2, since case 1 lacks a break
Case 1, then falls through into case 2
quiz.explanation: Colon-style cases fall through: without a break, control runs from case 1 straight into case 2 until the break there. It does not stop after case 1, it does not skip case 1, and default is not involved. The arrow form never falls through, which is why new code prefers it.

quiz.prompt: How does a multi-statement arm of a switch EXPRESSION return its value?
choices: `yield`
`return`
`break value`
`continue`
quiz.explanation: yield hands the value of a block arm back to the switch expression. return would leave the enclosing method instead of producing a value, continue belongs to loops, and "break value" was only a preview syntax in Java 12 that was replaced by yield. Single-expression arms need neither.

quiz.prompt: A switch expression over an enum lists every constant and has no default. A new constant is added later. What happens?
choices: It compiles and silently returns null for the new constant
It compiles, and the new constant falls through to the last arm
The switch stops compiling until the new constant is handled
It compiles with a warning that the switch is not exhaustive
quiz.explanation: A switch expression must be exhaustive, and for an enum without default the compiler checks that every constant has an arm. A new constant makes the switch fail to compile, which points you at every place to update. It does not return null, fall into another arm or merely warn; a default arm would hide the new constant.

quiz.prompt: `static void show(Object obj) { if (!(obj instanceof Integer n)) return; System.out.println(n + 1); }` What does `show(41)` do?
choices: Prints 42: n stays in scope after the negated check returns
Fails to compile: n is only in scope inside the if statement
Prints 411: n + 1 concatenates because obj is an Object
Throws ClassCastException when n is read after the if
quiz.explanation: A pattern variable is in scope wherever the match is definitely true. After `if (!(obj instanceof Integer n)) return;` the rest of the method only runs when the match succeeded, so n is an Integer there and n + 1 is arithmetic, printing 42.

quiz.prompt: What happens when you switch on a String variable that is null (Java 17)?
choices: NullPointerException
The default arm runs
It is treated as ""
A compile error
quiz.explanation: On Java 17 a switch on a null String throws NullPointerException before any arm is chosen, so even a default arm does not catch it. Check for null before switching. (Java 21 adds `case null` to pattern switches; 17 has no such arm.)

quiz.prompt: What does `sealed interface R permits A, B {}` guarantee?
choices: A and B are implicitly made final by the compiler
R and its permitted subtypes are all immutable
A and B must be records declared in the same file as R
A and B are the only permitted direct subtypes
quiz.explanation: sealed ... permits A, B makes A and B the only allowed direct subtypes, so the compiler and tools can reason about every case. It does not make them final by itself: each must declare final, sealed or non-sealed. Sealing says nothing about immutability, and the subtypes need not be records or live in the same file.

quiz.prompt: How do you leave BOTH of two nested loops at once?
choices: Two break statements on one line
continue outer; from the inner loop
A labelled break: break outer;
It is impossible without return
quiz.explanation: Label the outer loop (`outer: for (...)`) and write `break outer;` inside the inner loop to leave both at once. `continue outer;` jumps to the next outer iteration instead of leaving, and a second break on the same line is never reached.

quiz.prompt: Which form of switch should new code prefer?
choices: The arrow form: no fall-through, usable as an expression
The colon form, which compiles to a faster jump table
Chained if/else, since switch cannot match on strings
The colon form: the arrow form is still in preview
quiz.explanation: The arrow form cannot fall through, so the forgotten-break bug is gone, and it can be used as an expression that produces a value. The colon form is not faster, switch has matched strings since Java 7, and the arrow form left preview in Java 14. Prefer arrows in new code.

choices: A try/catch wrapped around the whole method that swallows bad input
An early return for a special case so the main path stays flat
A synchronized block that guards shared state in the method
A default arm that catches every value no case matched
quiz.explanation: A guard clause handles a special case first and returns early, so the main path is not nested inside if/else. Handling not-found and conflict cases at the top keeps the happy path flat and readable. It is not a try/catch that swallows input, a synchronized block or a default switch arm.

flashcards.back: Arrow arms never fall through and can form an expression; colon cases fall through until a break.
It produces the value of a block arm inside a switch expression.

flashcards.front: Why list every enum constant instead of using default?
flashcards.back: The compiler then reports every switch that misses a newly added constant.

flashcards.front: Pattern matching for instanceof in one line
flashcards.back: It tests the runtime type and binds a variable of that type, replacing a separate cast.
Throws NullPointerException; test for null before the switch.

flashcards.front: What does sealed add to an interface?
flashcards.back: An explicit, closed list of permitted subtypes known to the compiler.
Breaking to a label on an outer loop exits all the nested loops in one step.
Returning early for special cases keeps the main logic at one level of indentation.

drills.title: Switch expressions and instanceof patterns
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our shipping fee is a chain of if/else with a missing branch for pickup orders, and the logger prints useless toString output for values. Rewrite both."

**Why it matters.** A switch expression over an enum is checked for exhaustiveness, and instanceof patterns replace test-and-cast pairs.

**Your task.** Implement two methods (`Tier` is a nested enum):
- `static long shippingCents(Tier tier, long orderCents)` with a switch expression:
  - `STANDARD`: 499, but free (0) when `orderCents` is at least 5000
  - `EXPRESS`: 1299, halved (649, integer division) when `orderCents` is at least 10000
  - `PICKUP`: 0
- `static String describe(Object value)` with instanceof patterns:
  - `null` → `"null"`
  - an `Integer` → `"int " + value`
  - a `String` that is blank → `"blank string"`, otherwise `"string of length " + length`
  - a `List<?>` → `"list of " + size + " items"`
  - anything else → `"other " + simple class name`

**Worked example.** `shippingCents(Tier.EXPRESS, 12000)` is 649; `describe(List.of(1, 2))` is `"list of 2 items"`.
hints: A switch expression over the enum can hold the three fee rules, and patterns in instanceof checks avoid casts.
Use one switch expression over the tier with an arm per constant, and in the description rule out null first, then test each supported type with a pattern that binds the value.
Give each tier its own arm in one switch that produces the fee, and for the description check for null first and then each supported type in turn, falling back to the class name.

drills.title: Bug hunt: switch expressions and instanceof patterns
drills.instructions:
**Bug hunt.** The code in the editor is a plausible first attempt at drill 1, "Switch expressions and instanceof patterns". It passes some of the tests, but it has one real bug, the kind a reviewer should catch before it ships.

**Your task.** Find the bug and fix it, changing as little as you can; the tests are the same as drill 1's. The spec is unchanged: Implement two methods (`Tier` is a nested enum):
- `static long shippingCents(Tier tier, long orderCents)` with a switch expression:
  - `STANDARD`: 499, but free (0) when `orderCents` is at least 5000
  - `EXPRESS`: 1299, halved (649, integer division) when `orderCents` is at least 10000
  - `PICKUP`: 0
- `static String describe(Object value)` with instanceof patterns:
  - `null` → `"null"`
  - an `Integer` → `"int " + value`
  - a `String` that is blank → `"blank string"`, otherwise `"string of length " + length`
  - a `List<?>` → `"list of " + size + " items"`
  - anything else → `"other " + simple class name`
drills.explanation:
The planted bug is a boundary. `orderCents > 5000` charges 499 for an order of exactly 5000 cents, while the rule says shipping is free from 5000 up. "standard shipping and its free threshold" checks 4999 and 5000, so it fails on the second value, and every other test passes. The fix is one character:

```java
case STANDARD -> orderCents >= 5000 ? 0 : 499;
```

Boundaries in money rules are where bugs live, and the express arm already uses `>=` for its 10000-cent threshold. Adding a `default` arm or reordering the arms changes nothing here: the comparison is the bug, not the shape of the switch.
hints: What does an order of exactly 5000 cents pay for standard shipping?
The spec makes shipping free FROM the threshold, but the comparison only frees totals above it.
Include the threshold itself in the free range.
